text:
### Observed differences

- The elapsed time from a completion of A40 to the next completion of A15 roughly doubled: in the earlier window these intervals averaged about 2.0 hours (median about 2.0, middle half about 1.9–2.1 hours), while in the later window they averaged about 3.9 hours (median about 3.9, middle half about 3.6–4.3 hours) — an increase of about 1.9 hours per occurrence. [TWAIT001]
- The shift affects the whole distribution rather than a few long cases: every quartile rose by roughly 1.7–2.1 hours and the spread about doubled (standard deviation from about 0.25 to about 0.54 hours). [TWAIT001]
- The difference is far outside what random re-splits of the pooled data produce: only about 10 of 2000 random re-splits showed a larger difference. [TWAIT001]
- Slightly fewer A40→A15 consecutive completion intervals were observed in the later window (61 vs 69, from 200 traces per window). [TWAIT001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility of a timing change: the interval between consecutive completions of A40 and A15 lengthened from about 2 hours per occurrence in the earlier window to about 3.9 hours in the later window. The sign is direct (the indicator measures exactly this interval), the shift is consistent across the entire distribution, it rests on a substantial number of observations (69 and 61 intervals), and it exceeds about 999.5 in 1000 random re-splits. The screening comparison also fits a pure timing change: the time family produced 1 qualifying item where about 0.009 were expected without change (roughly a hundredfold excess), while the control-flow family produced 0 items where about 0.28 were expected, so no structural counterpart is needed and none was observed. [TWAIT001]

Limitations: TWAIT is elapsed time between consecutive completion events, so the evidence cannot show whether the extra ~1.9 hours is waiting, processing or idle time, and since only the A40–A15 pair was measured it cannot show whether the slowdown is specific to this interval or part of a broader timing shift. A competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is a changed mix of cases between the windows; the distribution-wide, consistent shift makes pure sampling variation unlikely, but a single measured pair limits how far the conclusion generalises. [TWAIT001]

Other differences: none beyond the slightly lower number of observed A40–A15 intervals in the later window (61 vs 69), which, given no qualifying control-flow items, may reflect sampling variation rather than a participation change. [TWAIT001]

Let me analyse this evidence.

Screening: 74 units tested, 0.29 items expected without change. By family:
- control_flow: 56 units tested, 0 items, 0.28 expected
- time: 18 units tested, 1 item, 0.009 expected

So the time family has 1 item when 0.009 expected. That's about 111 times the expectation. Per the instructions: "A count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole". So the screening comparison suggests the single time item is unusual — 1 item vs 0.009 expected is many times larger. So we don't automatically go to "Insufficient evidence" via the screening count comparison.

Wait, let me re-read: "A count of the same order as that expectation (for example one or two items when fewer than one is expected) is what an unchanged process typically produces: choose 'Insufficient evidence', however large or unusual a single item looks."

Hmm, this is tricky. "one or two items when fewer than one is expected" — here we have 1 item when 0.009 is expected. 0.009 is fewer than one. So 1 item when fewer than one is expected... but the example says "one or two items when fewer than one is expected" is what an unchanged process typically produces. But 0.009 expected means the probability of at least 1 item by chance is about 0.9%. That's quite unusual. The example in the instructions seems to be about expectations like 0.28 (control flow) where 1 item is plausible. But 0.009 expected — 1 item is ~111x the expectation.

The instruction says "A count many times larger cannot be explained by chance as a whole". 1 vs 0.009 is many times larger (111x). So the screening comparison passes — the count is not of the same order as the expectation.

Hmm, but there's tension: "for example one or two items when fewer than one is expected" — that example literally covers 1 item when 0.009 is expected. But 0.009 is very different from, say, 0.5. The example probably intends expectations close to 1 (like 0.28 or 0.5), where 1-2 items is within chance. With 0.009 expected, getting 1 item has probability ~0.9% under no change. The empirical_strength of 0.9995 also supports that this difference is unusual for random splits (only 0.05% of reference comparisons show a larger difference).

I think the intent: the screening comparison is the first gate. 1 item vs 0.009 expected is many times larger, so we proceed to judge by directness, consistency, etc. The control_flow family has 0 items vs 0.28 expected — consistent with no control-flow change.

Now the single item: TWAIT001, T_WAIT between A40 and A15 (consecutive completion events). Before: 69 components, mean ~2.0 hours, std ~0.25h, median ~2.02h. After: 61 components, mean ~3.86 hours, std ~0.54h, median ~3.91h. Difference in mean: +1.86 hours. Empirical strength 0.9995 — very unusual for random splits. Support: 69 before, 61 after — decent number of observations (out of 200 traces each).

The characterization says "redistributed" with all components increased except count decreased. So the elapsed time between consecutive completions of A40→A15 roughly doubled from ~2h to ~3.9h, and the count of such consecutive pairs decreased slightly (69 → 61).

Per instructions: "TWAIT is the elapsed time between consecutive completion events; do not call it pure waiting, service or processing time. A consistent change in these times is a hypothesis in its own right (a change in timing); it does not need a structural counterpart."

So this is a timing hypothesis: the elapsed time between A40 completion and A15 completion increased from about 2 hours to about 3.9 hours.

Is this "Supported hypothesis" or "Weak hypothesis"?

Judging criteria: directness, consistency, ability to rule out competing explanations.

- Directness: TWAIT directly measures the elapsed time between the two events. The change is direct evidence of timing change.

Competing explanations: Could this be a rare-variant artifact? The support counts (69, 61) are substantial, so not a rare variant.
